passage: Yosef's slides were ready, but his hands weren't. In the small seminar room in Haifa he stood beside the screen with a line graph of monthly rainfall and heard Noa in the second row whisper, "Slow down." He took a breath. When he reached the rise in spring, he drew his right hand upward in a smooth slant, then flattened it for the dry summer. It matched the picture. But when nervous, his left hand kept flicking a marker cap, and Noa saw two students watching that instead. After the talk she said, "The slope gesture was great. The flicking was distracting." He laughed and set the marker on the table. Next time he would record himself first.

qa.q: What did Yosef's graph show?
qa.a: The graph showed monthly rainfall.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling as he presented, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Yosef was nervous, because his left hand kept flicking a marker cap. He was still able to use a clear slanting hand for the spring rise, which suggests he was also focused on explaining.

qa.q: What could Yosef do before the next talk?
qa.a: Record himself presenting on video, keep the gestures that match the graph and trim the marker flicking.

qa.q: How did Noa see the two kinds of hand movement?
qa.a: Noa found the slope gesture helpful and the flicking distracting, and noticed two students watching the flicking instead of the graph.

grounding: A young adult uses measured hand shapes to show a graph trend, while fidgety motions distract, and rehearsing on video helps.

passage: Dolma's turn in the lab meeting came after lunch. The supervisor, Dr. Mehta, had asked each student to explain their work in three minutes. She walked to the whiteboard and traced a rising curve with one finger, then made a small circle with both hands to show how the sample cycled through the machine. Anirban, sitting near the door, followed easily. Then her arms began to swing wide with every sentence, and he found himself watching the hands, not the diagram. Dr. Mehta wrote something down. After the meeting she showed Dolma a phone video from last week's practice. "See how the big swings start here?" Dolma winced, then grinned and said she'd keep the circle and cut the rest.

qa.q: How long did the supervisor give each student to explain their work?
qa.a: The supervisor gave each student three minutes.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when she watched the practice video?
qa.a: Dolma winced first, probably embarrassed, then grinned, which suggests she took the feedback well and felt ready to change. The grin could also be relief at having a clear thing to fix.

qa.q: What went wrong in the second half of the talk, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The wide arm swings drew attention from the diagram; Dolma could keep the meaningful gestures and rehearse on video to trim the rest.

qa.q: What was it like for Anirban listening to the talk?
qa.a: Anirban followed the early gestures easily, but as the arms began to swing wide he found himself watching the hands instead of the diagram.

grounding: A young adult uses purposeful hand shapes in a presentation, over-large motions distract, and video rehearsal shows what to trim.

passage:
Dear Harish,
You asked how the thesis presentation went. Better than the rehearsal, and I owe that to the video you told me to take.
When I watched it on Sunday I nearly deleted it. My arms were windmilling on every sentence. At one point I flung my hand so wide I knocked the pointer off the table. You could not look at the slides for all the waving.
So I planned my gestures like slides. For the rise in the rainfall graph, one flat hand climbing slowly. For the three stages of the filter, three fingers, one at a time. Everything else, hands resting loosely on the lectern.
On Tuesday Professor Roy followed the graph with her eyes when my hand rose, and nodded. My hands still twitched once or twice, but it felt like they were helping.
Thanks for the push,
Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila knock off the table in the rehearsal video?
qa.a: The pointer.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when first watching the rehearsal video?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed enough to nearly delete it, seeing the windmilling arms; there is also some relief later, as the video showed exactly what to change.

qa.q: What went wrong in the rehearsal, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Large, constant arm movements pulled attention away from the slides; planning a few purposeful gestures and resting the hands otherwise fixed it.

qa.q: How does Professor Roy seem to experience the final presentation?
qa.a: She follows the graph with her eyes as Sharmila's hand rises and nods, so the gesture helped her understand instead of distracting her.

grounding: Shows a young adult trimming over-large gestures after watching a rehearsal video and using purposeful hand shapes to show a graph and a process.

passage: Nikita, you know me, Kalyani, the girl who talks with her whole body. So picture my final-year presentation on the metro line plan. I was so nervous I was waving both hands like I was directing traffic. And I noticed Dr Menon wasn't looking at my slides at all. His eyes kept following my hands, left, right, up. Awful. That night I propped my phone on a stack of books and recorded myself. Honestly, watching it, I cringed. There was one good gesture, though. When I said the line would curve round the lake, my hand drew the curve slowly, and it actually made sense. So I kept that, and one for 'three stations', and I made myself rest my hands on the table for the rest. At the second round, Dr Menon asked a question about the lake curve. He'd been following.

qa.q: Where did Kalyani prop the phone to record herself?
qa.a: On a stack of books.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she noticed Dr Menon's eyes following her hands?
qa.a: She felt awful and embarrassed, seeing he was watching her hands instead of her slides; the waving itself also suggests she was nervous.

qa.q: What could someone like Kalyani try before a big presentation?
qa.a: Record a rehearsal, keep the gestures that clearly show an idea, like drawing a curve, and rest the hands the rest of the time.

qa.q: What was it like for Dr Menon during the first round?
qa.a: He seemed pulled away from the slides because his eyes kept following her hands; by the second round he was following the content well enough to ask about the curve.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing that busy gestures distract a listener and keeping only purposeful ones after recording a rehearsal.

passage: I'm Nirmala, and I sat in the second row for Chetan's lab presentation on water recycling. He's usually quiet, so I watched him closely. His first two minutes were rough: he kept jingling his keys in one pocket, and the girl next to me started tapping her pen to the same rhythm. I couldn't tell if he was nervous or just used to it. Then he reached the recycling loop. He drew a slow circle in the air with one hand and stopped at four points around it, naming each stage. Suddenly the whole room was looking where his hand was. After that his hand stayed out of his pocket. Later I asked if he'd practised. He shrugged and said he'd filmed himself twice and cut out "the key thing". Whether he felt calm by the end, I don't know, but he looked it.

qa.q: What did Chetan keep jingling in his pocket?
qa.a: His keys.

qa.q: What might Chetan have been feeling during the first two minutes?
qa.a: He may have been nervous, which the key-jingling suggests; Nirmala notes it could also just be a habit, so she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What small step had helped Chetan improve his gestures?
qa.a: Filming himself twice, which let him cut the key jingling and keep a clear circle gesture for the recycling loop.

qa.q: How did the audience experience the circle gesture compared with the jingling keys?
qa.a: The jingling pulled attention away and even set a pen tapping, while the circle made the whole room look where his hand was and follow the loop.

grounding: Shows through an observer how purposeful gestures help listeners follow a process while fidgety movements distract.

passage:
Friday: Aadhya filmed herself rehearsing her internship presentation on city bus ridership. Watching it back with her flatmate Vidya, she groaned. Her hands flew everywhere: circling, chopping, tugging her sleeve, even while she read out the numbers. "I can't follow the graph because I'm following your wrists," Vidya said, laughing.
Sunday: They chose three gestures only. A slow rising slope of the hand for the morning climb in riders, a flat palm for the midday plateau, and two hands pulling apart for the gap between weekdays and weekends. The rest of the time Aadhya let her hands rest at her sides. It felt stiff, like wearing someone else's shoes.
Wednesday: In the conference room, as she traced the rising line with one steady hand, she saw the regional manager's eyes follow it to the screen. Afterwards he said, "That slope stuck with me." Aadhya walked out grinning and messaged Vidya straight away.

qa.q: What gesture did Aadhya use for the midday plateau?
qa.a: A flat palm.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel about the trimmed gestures on Sunday?
qa.a: She felt awkward and stiff, "like wearing someone else's shoes", even though she could see that fewer gestures would be clearer.

qa.q: What made the video rehearsal useful?
qa.a: Watching it back showed which movements distracted, so Aadhya could keep three purposeful gestures and drop the rest.

qa.q: How did the regional manager experience the final presentation?
qa.a: He followed her steady rising hand to the screen and remembered the slope, so the gesture helped him grasp the trend.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using a video rehearsal to trim distracting hand movements and keep a few purposeful gestures that help listeners follow a graph.
